q: What is Git, at its core?
why: Git tracks changes to files over time. GitHub is the platform built around Git.

q: Where must GitHub Actions workflow files live?
why: Anything else and GitHub simply will not see it.

q: Workflow files are written in which format?
why: YAML — indentation matters, and it will absolutely bite you.
Continuous Integration: merge often, verify automatically.

q: Which key defines WHEN a workflow runs?
A runner starts empty. Which action puts your code on it?
why: Forget checkout and your build fails with 'no such file or directory'.

q: By default, multiple JOBS in one workflow run…
a: One after another, top to bottom
why: Jobs are parallel by default. Steps inside a job are sequential.

q: Which key makes job `deploy` wait for job `test`?
why: needs: builds the dependency graph between jobs.

why: frontend/ + api/ + worker/ + shared/ — one history, one PR.

q: How do you reference a repository secret in a workflow?
why: Never hardcode it. GitHub also masks the value in logs.

q: Which key stops a monorepo workflow from running on unrelated changes?
why: on.push.paths — the single highest-ROI line in a monorepo CI config.

A webhook to an external service

q: You change `shared/types.ts`, used by frontend, api and worker. Path filters on only `api/**` will…
a: Run nothing — a silent gap that ships a broken build
Fail the workflow with an error
why: This is the hard case: shared code needs fan-out filters, a changes-detection job, or a real build graph (Nx/Turborepo/Bazel).

a: Runs the same job many times across combinations (OS × version)
Splits a job across many repos
why: One job definition → node 18/20/22 × ubuntu/macos/windows, all in parallel.

q: In a monorepo, which CD strategy is usually the most efficient?
a: Rebuild and redeploy every service on every merge
Deploy only the services whose code (or dependencies) actually changed
Give every service its own repository again
why: Change detection + a dependency graph. Deploy the blast radius, nothing more.
